title: Intuition
text:
Imagine this: You’re given 1,000 unlabeled animal photos and asked: “How many different types of animals are there, and which photos go together?” This is exactly the clustering problem!
K-means answers this question by making a simplifying assumption: each type of animal can be represented by an average image (prototype), and each photo is close to one of these prototypes.






Important



Key Concept: Unsupervised Learning Clustering is unsupervised: no labels, no teacher to say “this is a cat.” The algorithm must discover the structure by itself.







flowchart TD
    A[Unlabeled data] --> B{Clustering problem}
    B --> C[k-means approach:<br/>find K centers<br/>and assign each point<br/>to the nearest center]
    B --> D[Hierarchical approach:<br/>build a tree<br/>of groupings]
    C --> E[Advantage: simple, fast]
    D --> F[Advantage: visualization<br/>via dendrogram]

    style E fill:#e6f3ff
    style F fill:#e6ffe6









Analogy: Imagine a game of musical chairs with K chairs (clusters) and N players (data points). When the music stops: 1. Each player runs to the nearest chair (assignment) 2. Each chair is moved to the center of the players surrounding it (update) 3. Repeat until the chairs no longer move
This is exactly k-means!





flowchart TD
    A[K chairs placed<br/>randomly] --> B[Music stops:<br/>each player runs<br/>to the nearest chair]
    B --> C[Move each chair<br/>to the center of<br/>surrounding players]
    C --> D{Did the chairs<br/>move much?}
    D -->|Yes, repeat| B
    D -->|No, game over| E[Result: K groups<br/>of players]











K-means seeks to minimize:
L = sum over all points of (distance to its cluster center)²
Why squared? Two reasons: 1. Mathematical: makes the problem easier to solve 2. Geometric: penalizes more points that are very far away



Assignment step (E-like): For each point x_i, find the nearest center μ_k:
Assign x_i to cluster k that minimizes ||x_i - μ_k||²
Update step (M-like): For each cluster k, recalculate its center:
μ_k = average of all points assigned to cluster k






Note



Why does it converge? Each step can only improve (or leave unchanged) the criterion. Since there’s a finite number of possible assignments, the algorithm must terminate.








If all chairs start in the same corner, the game will be very long and yield a poor result. K-means is very sensitive to initialization!





flowchart TD
    A[Initialization choice] --> B[Poor initialization]
    A --> C[Good initialization]
    B --> D[Slow convergence<br/>Poor quality clusters<br/>Local maximum]
    C --> E[Fast convergence<br/>Good quality clusters<br/>Global (or good) maximum]

    style D fill:#ffcccc
    style E fill:#ccffcc









Principle: Spread out the initial centers from each other.
Algorithm: 1. Choose a first center at random 2. For each point, calculate its distance D(x) to the nearest center 3. Choose the next center with probability proportional to D(x)² 4. Repeat until K centers are chosen
Why does it work? By favoring distant points, we better cover the data space.






Tip



Practical tip: Always use k-means++ or run k-means multiple times with different random initializations and keep the best result.








K-means needs to be told how many clusters to look for. But in real life, we don’t know in advance!





Principle: Plot the error (inertia) as a function of K.
Error(K) = sum of squared distances from points to their center
As K increases, the error decreases. We look for the “elbow” where improvement slows down.



Principle: Measures how well a point fits in its cluster vs. outside its cluster.
s(i) = (b(i) - a(i)) / max(a(i), b(i))
where a(i) = average distance to other points in the same cluster, b(i) = average distance to points in the nearest other cluster.
Interpretation: s(i) ≈ 1 = well classified, ≈ 0 = on the border, ≈ -1 = misclassified.



For N points: K ≈ √(N/2) (very rough, use with caution).













Aspect
K-means
GMM with EM




Philosophy
Geometric (distance)
Probabilistic (density)


Membership
Hard (0 or 1)
Soft (probability)


Cluster shape
Spheres (all same size)
Ellipses (variable sizes/orientations)


Model
Minimizes distance
Maximizes likelihood


Speed
Fast (O(NKT))
Slower (more calculations)


Limit case
-
K-means = GMM with σ→0 and spherical covariances









Important



K-means is a special case of GMM! When we take a Gaussian mixture with: - Spherical and identical covariances: Σ_k = σ²I - And let σ → 0 Then soft assignment becomes hard, and we recover k-means.







Problem: K-means assumes spherical clusters. If they’re elongated or oddly shaped, it fails.
Solution: - Standardize the data (center and scale) - Use another method (GMM, spectral clustering) - Transform the data (PCA first)



Problem: K-means tends to create clusters of similar size, even if reality is different.
Solution: Adjust K, or use a method that handles this (GMM).



Problem: A very distant point pulls its cluster center toward it.
Solution: - Detect and remove outliers beforehand - Use k-medoids (more robust) - Standardize to reduce influence



Problem: K-means always finds K clusters, even if the data has no structure.
Solution: Always validate with objective methods (silhouette, gap statistic).







Clean: handle missing values
Standardize: center and scale each variable
Visualize (if possible in 2D/3D) to get an idea





Elbow method: plot inertia vs K
Silhouette score: average over all points
Domain knowledge: sometimes we know how many clusters to look for




# Pseudocode
1. Initialize K centers with k-means++
2. Repeat:
   a. Assign each point to the nearest center
   b. Recalculate centers as averages
   c. If centers move little, stop
3. Evaluate with silhouette score
4. If in doubt, rerun with different initializations




Internal: scores (silhouette, Davies-Bouldin)
External: if you have some labels, compare
Manual: visualization, common sense







Difference: Centers are actual data points (not averages).
Advantage: More robust to outliers, works with any distance.



Difference: Uses data subsamples at each iteration.
Advantage: Much faster for large datasets.



Difference: Soft assignment (like GMM) but with a geometric criterion.
Advantage: Border points belong partially to multiple clusters.










Important



In 30 seconds for the oral exam:

K-means = clustering by distance minimization
Two steps: assignment (points → nearest center) and update (recalculate centers)
Problems: choice of K, initialization, spherical clusters
Solutions: k-means++, elbow method, standardization
Relationship: special case of GMM with σ→0
Applications: segmentation, grouping, dimensionality reduction






“Imagine organizing a party with guests scattered in a park. You want to create K discussion groups. You place K facilitators randomly (initialization), each guest joins the nearest facilitator (assignment), then the facilitators move to the center of their group (update). You repeat until the facilitators no longer move. This is exactly k-means!”



Q: “Why is k-means sensitive to initialization?” A: “Because the criterion to minimize has multiple local minima. Depending on where you start, you can get stuck in a bad minimum.”
Q: “How to choose K if you have no idea?” A: “Use the elbow method to see where improvement slows down, and validate with the silhouette score. Test several K values and see what makes sense for your data.”
Q: “When not to use k-means?” A: “When your clusters aren’t spherical, or have very different sizes, or when you have a lot of noise/outliers.”



K-means is like a Swiss Army knife for clustering: simple, fast, useful in many situations. But like any simple tool, you need to know its limitations. The key is to always: 1. Prepare your data (clean, standardize) 2. Choose K intelligently (elbow method, silhouette) 3. Initialize properly (k-means++) 4. Validate the results (visualization, scores)
In summary: K-means is your first tool for exploring the structure of unlabeled data. Not the most sophisticated, but often the most practical to start with.

title: Educational Course: Clustering and the k-means Algorithm
text:
Imagine you’re looking at the starry sky. Some stars seem naturally grouped into constellations. No one told you which stars form the Big Dipper - you see it for yourself.
This is exactly what clustering is: discovering natural groups in data, without prior guidance.







k-means seeks to accomplish two simultaneous objectives:

Find K representative centers
Assign each point to the nearest center

But how do we judge if we’ve succeeded?







Let’s measure how far each point is from the center of its group. The smaller this distance, the better the grouping.
For the entire dataset, we calculate:
\[
\text{Total error} = \sum_{\text{all points}} (\text{distance to its group center})^2
\]



Let’s define precisely:

Data: \(N\) points \(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, ..., \mathbf{x}_N\) in a \(D\)-dimensional space
Clusters: \(K\) groups (number chosen in advance)
Centers: \(\mu_1, \mu_2, ..., \mu_K\) (to be determined)
Assignment: For each point \(i\) and cluster \(k\), \(z_{ik} = 1\) if point \(i\) is in cluster \(k\), \(0\) otherwise




The objective function (or cost function) is:
\[
J = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{k=1}^{K} z_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2
\]
Let’s break down this formula:








Symbol
Meaning
Role in the formula




\(z_{ik}\)
Assignment indicator
Selects only the cluster to which the point belongs


\(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2\)
Squared distance
Measures how far the point is from the center


\(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\)
Sum over all points
Accumulates error for the entire dataset


\(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\)
Sum over all clusters
Considers all possible clusters



In practice: Since each point belongs to only one cluster, for a point \(\mathbf{x}_i\), only one \(z_{ik}\) equals 1, the others equal 0. So for each point, we only count the distance to its own center.







If we fix the assignments \(z_{ik}\), then for each cluster \(k\):
\[
J_k = \sum_{i: z_{ik}=1} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2
\]
This is exactly the variance of the points in cluster \(k\), multiplied by the number of points.
Minimizing \(J\) = Minimizing intra-cluster variance = Making clusters more compact



If we differentiate \(J\) with respect to \(\mu_k\):
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mu_k} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik} (\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k)
\]
Setting the derivative equal to zero:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik} (\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k) = 0
\]
\[
\Rightarrow \mu_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik} \mathbf{x}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik}}
\]
Interpretation: The optimal center is the mean (center of gravity) of the points in the cluster.



This function corresponds to the log-likelihood of a model where each cluster is a spherical Gaussian with the same variance.







We have two types of variables:

The assignments \(z_{ik}\) (discrete, binary variables)
The centers \(\mu_k\) (continuous variables)

The combinatorial problem is NP-hard: impossible to test all combinations.



Instead of optimizing all variables simultaneously, we alternate:

Optimize assignments while fixing centers
Optimize centers while fixing assignments






flowchart TD
    A[Center initialization] --> B
    
    subgraph B [E-step: Optimal Assignment]
        B1[Centers fixed] --> B2[For each point]
        B2 --> B3[Find nearest center]
        B3 --> B4[Assign point to this center]
    end
    
    B --> C
    
    subgraph C [M-step: Center Update]
        C1[Assignments fixed] --> C2[For each cluster]
        C2 --> C3[Calculate mean of points]
        C3 --> C4[Move center to this mean]
    end
    
    C --> D{Convergence?}
    D -- No --> B
    D -- Yes --> E[Final result]













Assumption: The centers \(\mu_1, ..., \mu_K\) are fixed.
Objective: Choose the \(z_{ik}\) to minimize \(J\).
Observation: The function \(J\) is a sum of positive terms. To minimize a sum, we minimize each term individually.
For a given point \(\mathbf{x}_i\), we must choose a single \(k\) such that \(z_{ik} = 1\). The corresponding term is \(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2\).
Optimal solution: Assign \(\mathbf{x}_i\) to the nearest center!
Formally:
\[
z_{ik} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } k = \arg\min_{j} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_j\|^2 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
Complexity: For each point (N), compare with each center (K) → \(O(N \times K \times D)\) operations.



Assumption: The assignments \(z_{ik}\) are fixed.
Objective: Choose the \(\mu_k\) to minimize \(J\).
Calculation: As seen previously, by differentiating with respect to \(\mu_k\):
\[
\mu_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik} \mathbf{x}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik}}
\]
Interpretation: The new center of cluster \(k\) is the mean (centroid) of all points assigned to it.
Complexity: For each cluster (K), average its points → \(O(N \times D)\) operations.












graph LR
    A[Iteration t] --> B[E-step: better assignment]
    B --> C[Error decreases or stays same]
    C --> D[M-step: better centers]
    D --> E[Error decreases or stays same]
    E --> F[Iteration t+1 with error ≤ previous error]
    
    style C fill:#dfd
    style E fill:#dfd










E-step: For fixed centers \(\mu_k^{(t)}\), choosing \(z_{ik}^{(t+1)}\) as the optimal assignment guarantees: \[
J(\mu^{(t)}, z^{(t+1)}) \leq J(\mu^{(t)}, z^{(t)})
\] (strictly less if an assignment changes)
M-step: For fixed assignments \(z_{ik}^{(t+1)}\), choosing \(\mu_k^{(t+1)}\) as the optimal means guarantees: \[
J(\mu^{(t+1)}, z^{(t+1)}) \leq J(\mu^{(t)}, z^{(t+1)})
\] (strictly less if a center changes)
Conclusion: At each complete iteration (E then M), the error can only decrease: \[
J^{(t+1)} \leq J^{(t)}
\]




Since the error is always positive and decreases with each iteration, the algorithm necessarily converges.







Imagine you’re looking for the lowest point in a mountainous region, blindfolded. You always go downhill. You’ll end up in a valley, but not necessarily in the lowest valley!
This is exactly what happens to k-means:





graph TD
    A[Random start] --> B{Which valley?}
    B --> C[Deep valley<br>Global optimum]
    B --> D[Less deep valley<br>Local minimum]
    
    C --> E[Good solution]
    D --> F[Poor solution]
    
    style C fill:#9f9
    style D fill:#f99









The function \(J\) is not convex with respect to all variables. It has several “valleys” (local minima).
Concrete example: With 4 points forming a square, and K=2, there are two equivalent solutions:

Solution 1: Cluster {(1,2)}, Cluster {(3,4)}
Solution 2: Cluster {(1,3)}, Cluster {(2,4)}

Both give the same value of \(J\), but they are different local minima.







Rather than choosing initial centers completely randomly, choose them in a way that “covers” the data space.




First center: Chosen uniformly at random from all points
For each subsequent center:

For each point \(\mathbf{x}_i\), calculate: \[
D(\mathbf{x}_i) = \min_{\text{centers already chosen}} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_j\|^2
\] (Squared distance to the nearest center already chosen)
Choose the next center with probability proportional to \(D(\mathbf{x}_i)^2\) \[
P(\text{choose } \mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{D(\mathbf{x}_i)^2}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} D(\mathbf{x}_j)^2}
\]

Repeat until K centers





Points far from existing centers have a higher probability of being chosen
This guarantees that initial centers are spread out throughout the space
In practice, this gives better results than purely random initialization








k-means assumes that each cluster approximately follows a normal (Gaussian) distribution with:

Spherical shape: The covariance is \(\sigma^2 I\) (same in all directions)
Same variance: All clusters have the same “spread”
Different centers: Each cluster has its own center \(\mu_k\)




If each cluster \(k\) is modeled by a Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \sigma^2 I)\), then the probability density is:
\[
p(\mathbf{x} | \text{cluster } k) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{D/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mu_k\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
\]



Consider the log-likelihood of the data:
\[
\log p(\mathcal{X} | \{\mu_k\}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k p(\mathbf{x}_i | \mu_k, \sigma^2 I)\right)
\]
With \(\pi_k = 1/K\) (equiprobable clusters).
Limiting case: When \(\sigma^2 \to 0\) (very “peaked” distributions), the dominant term in the sum is that of the nearest cluster.
We then obtain approximately:
\[
\log p(\mathcal{X} | \{\mu_k\}) \approx \text{constant} - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \min_k \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2
\]
Maximizing this likelihood is equivalent to minimizing:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \min_k \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2
\]
Which is exactly the function \(J\) of k-means!



k-means can be viewed as an EM algorithm for a mixture of spherical Gaussians with the same variance, taking the limit where the distributions are infinitely “peaked” (hard assignment).








k-means minimizes: The sum of squared distances between each point and its cluster center
Optimization method: Alternation between two simple steps:

Assignment: Each point joins the nearest center
Update: Each center becomes the mean of its points

Guaranteed property: Error decreases at each iteration until convergence
Main limitation: Converges to a local minimum, not necessarily global
Key improvement: k-means++ for better initialization

    Method

What happens if we change the metric? (From Euclidean distance to Manhattan distance)
How to adapt k-means for clusters with different densities?
Why not minimize the sum of distances (not squared)?




Mentally try this exercise:

Take 6 points forming two equilateral triangles
Apply k-means with K=2
Observe how initialization influences the final result






k-means is like a conductor organizing musicians (the points) into sections (clusters) by placing each musician near the section leader (center) while keeping sections apart from each other.
The beauty of the algorithm lies in its simplicity: a simple idea (minimize distances), an effective method (alternation), and interpretable results.
Remember: Understanding the objective function and its optimization is the key to using k-means wisely and correctly interpreting its results!

Centers: \(\mu_1, \mu_2, ..., \mu_K\) (to be determined)
Assignment: For each point \(i\) and cluster \(k\), \(z_{ik} = 1\) if point \(i\) is in cluster \(k\), \(0\) otherwise




The objective function (or cost function) is:
\[
J = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{k=1}^{K} z_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2
\]
Let’s break down this formula:








Symbol
Meaning
Role in the formula




\(z_{ik}\)
Assignment indicator
Selects only the cluster to which the point belongs


\(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2\)
Squared distance
Measures how far the point is from the center


\(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\)
Sum over all points
Accumulates error for the entire dataset


\(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\)
Sum over all clusters
Considers all possible clusters



In practice: Since each point belongs to only one cluster, for a point \(\mathbf{x}_i\), only one \(z_{ik}\) equals 1, the others equal 0. So for each point, we only count the distance to its own center.
crumbs: Educational Course: Clustering and the k-means Algorithm

title: Educational Course: Clustering and the k-means Algorithm
text:
If we fix the assignments \(z_{ik}\), then for each cluster \(k\):
\[
J_k = \sum_{i: z_{ik}=1} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2
\]
This is exactly the variance of the points in cluster \(k\), multiplied by the number of points.
Minimizing \(J\) = Minimizing intra-cluster variance = Making clusters more compact



If we differentiate \(J\) with respect to \(\mu_k\):
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mu_k} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik} (\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k)
\]
Setting the derivative equal to zero:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik} (\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k) = 0
\]
\[
\Rightarrow \mu_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik} \mathbf{x}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik}}
\]
Interpretation: The optimal center is the mean (center of gravity) of the points in the cluster.



This function corresponds to the log-likelihood of a model where each cluster is a spherical Gaussian with the same variance.

title: Educational Course: Clustering and the k-means Algorithm
text:
We have two types of variables:

The assignments \(z_{ik}\) (discrete, binary variables)
The centers \(\mu_k\) (continuous variables)

The combinatorial problem is NP-hard: impossible to test all combinations.



Instead of optimizing all variables simultaneously, we alternate:

Optimize assignments while fixing centers
Optimize centers while fixing assignments

title: Educational Course: Clustering and the k-means Algorithm
text:
Assumption: The centers \(\mu_1, ..., \mu_K\) are fixed.
Objective: Choose the \(z_{ik}\) to minimize \(J\).
Observation: The function \(J\) is a sum of positive terms. To minimize a sum, we minimize each term individually.
For a given point \(\mathbf{x}_i\), we must choose a single \(k\) such that \(z_{ik} = 1\). The corresponding term is \(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2\).
Optimal solution: Assign \(\mathbf{x}_i\) to the nearest center!
Formally:
\[
z_{ik} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } k = \arg\min_{j} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_j\|^2 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
Complexity: For each point (N), compare with each center (K) → \(O(N \times K \times D)\) operations.



Assumption: The assignments \(z_{ik}\) are fixed.
Objective: Choose the \(\mu_k\) to minimize \(J\).
Calculation: As seen previously, by differentiating with respect to \(\mu_k\):
\[
\mu_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik} \mathbf{x}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_{ik}}
\]
Interpretation: The new center of cluster \(k\) is the mean (centroid) of all points assigned to it.
Complexity: For each cluster (K), average its points → \(O(N \times D)\) operations.

    C --> D[M-step: better centers]
    D --> E[Error decreases or stays same]
    E --> F[Iteration t+1 with error ≤ previous error]
    
    style C fill:#dfd
    style E fill:#dfd










E-step: For fixed centers \(\mu_k^{(t)}\), choosing \(z_{ik}^{(t+1)}\) as the optimal assignment guarantees: \[
J(\mu^{(t)}, z^{(t+1)}) \leq J(\mu^{(t)}, z^{(t)})
\] (strictly less if an assignment changes)
M-step: For fixed assignments \(z_{ik}^{(t+1)}\), choosing \(\mu_k^{(t+1)}\) as the optimal means guarantees: \[
J(\mu^{(t+1)}, z^{(t+1)}) \leq J(\mu^{(t)}, z^{(t+1)})
\] (strictly less if a center changes)
Conclusion: At each complete iteration (E then M), the error can only decrease: \[
J^{(t+1)} \leq J^{(t)}
\]




Since the error is always positive and decreases with each iteration, the algorithm necessarily converges.

Imagine you’re looking for the lowest point in a mountainous region, blindfolded. You always go downhill. You’ll end up in a valley, but not necessarily in the lowest valley!
This is exactly what happens to k-means:

The function \(J\) is not convex with respect to all variables. It has several “valleys” (local minima).
Concrete example: With 4 points forming a square, and K=2, there are two equivalent solutions:

Solution 1: Cluster {(1,2)}, Cluster {(3,4)}
Solution 2: Cluster {(1,3)}, Cluster {(2,4)}

Both give the same value of \(J\), but they are different local minima.

title: Educational Course: Clustering and the k-means Algorithm
text:
Rather than choosing initial centers completely randomly, choose them in a way that “covers” the data space.




First center: Chosen uniformly at random from all points
For each subsequent center:

For each point \(\mathbf{x}_i\), calculate: \[
D(\mathbf{x}_i) = \min_{\text{centers already chosen}} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_j\|^2
\] (Squared distance to the nearest center already chosen)
Choose the next center with probability proportional to \(D(\mathbf{x}_i)^2\) \[
P(\text{choose } \mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{D(\mathbf{x}_i)^2}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} D(\mathbf{x}_j)^2}
\]

Repeat until K centers





Points far from existing centers have a higher probability of being chosen
This guarantees that initial centers are spread out throughout the space
In practice, this gives better results than purely random initialization

title: Educational Course: Clustering and the k-means Algorithm
text:
k-means assumes that each cluster approximately follows a normal (Gaussian) distribution with:

Spherical shape: The covariance is \(\sigma^2 I\) (same in all directions)
Same variance: All clusters have the same “spread”
Different centers: Each cluster has its own center \(\mu_k\)




If each cluster \(k\) is modeled by a Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \sigma^2 I)\), then the probability density is:
\[
p(\mathbf{x} | \text{cluster } k) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{D/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mu_k\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
\]



Consider the log-likelihood of the data:
\[
\log p(\mathcal{X} | \{\mu_k\}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k p(\mathbf{x}_i | \mu_k, \sigma^2 I)\right)
\]
With \(\pi_k = 1/K\) (equiprobable clusters).
Limiting case: When \(\sigma^2 \to 0\) (very “peaked” distributions), the dominant term in the sum is that of the nearest cluster.
We then obtain approximately:
\[
\log p(\mathcal{X} | \{\mu_k\}) \approx \text{constant} - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \min_k \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2
\]
Maximizing this likelihood is equivalent to minimizing:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \min_k \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_k\|^2
\]
Which is exactly the function \(J\) of k-means!



k-means can be viewed as an EM algorithm for a mixture of spherical Gaussians with the same variance, taking the limit where the distributions are infinitely “peaked” (hard assignment).

Optimization method: Alternation between two simple steps:

Assignment: Each point joins the nearest center
Update: Each center becomes the mean of its points

Guaranteed property: Error decreases at each iteration until convergence
Main limitation: Converges to a local minimum, not necessarily global
Key improvement: k-means++ for better initialization

title: Exam questions
text:
Introduction: The Fundamental Idea
Imagine you’re looking at a starry sky. Some stars seem to cluster into constellations, others are isolated. The Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) is like a mathematical attempt to describe this sky: it models data as coming from several “constellations” (the Gaussian components) that overlap more or less.

title: Exam questions
section: 1. What is a Gaussian Mixture Model?
text:
1. What is a Gaussian Mixture Model?

Simple Definition
A GMM is a probabilistic model that represents a complex data distribution as a combination (a “mixture”) of several simpler Gaussian (normal) distributions.
Culinary analogy: Imagine cookie dough with two types of chocolate chips (dark and white). A GMM would try to model this dough as: - 60% dough with dark chips (one Gaussian) - 40% dough with white chips (another Gaussian)


Mathematical Formulation
A GMM with \(c\) components is written as:
\[
f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{c} \pi_j \mathcal{N}(x|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)
\]
Let’s break down each element:

\(f(x)\): The total probability density at point \(x\)
\(\sum_{j=1}^{c}\): The sum over all \(c\) components
\(\pi_j\): The weight of component \(j\) (its proportion in the mixture)
\(\mathcal{N}(x|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)\): A Gaussian (normal) distribution

title: Exam questions
text:
2. The Three Fundamental Assumptions

Assumption 1: Mixture Structure
Data is generated by a two-step process: 1. Drawing a component: Randomly choose a component \(j\) with probability \(\pi_j\) 2. Generating a point: Generate \(x\) according to the Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_j, \Sigma_j)\)
Analogy: To choose a candy from a bag: 1. First choose the type of candy (60% chance of being red, 40% of being blue) 2. Then draw a candy of that type


Assumption 2: Gaussian Shape of Components
Each component follows a multivariate normal distribution:
\[
\mathcal{N}(x|\mu_j, \Sigma_j) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2}|\Sigma_j|^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mu_j)^T \Sigma_j^{-1}(x - \mu_j)\right)
\]
Where: * \(D\) is the data dimension * \(|\Sigma_j|\) is the determinant of the matrix \(\Sigma_j\) * \((x - \mu_j)^T \Sigma_j^{-1}(x - \mu_j)\) is the Mahalanobis distance


Assumption 3: Conditional Independence
Observations are independent of each other given the components to which they belong.

title: Exam questions
text:
3. The Model Parameters
A GMM has three types of parameters to learn:

1. The Weights \(\pi_j\) (Mixing Weights)

What they are: The proportion of each component in the mixture
Constraints:

\(\sum_{j=1}^c \pi_j = 1\) (the sum equals 100%)
\(\pi_j \geq 0\) for all \(j\) (no negative weights)

Interpretation: If \(\pi_1 = 0.6\), it means 60% of the data (in probability) come from the first component



2. The Means \(\mu_j\)

What they are: The center of each Gaussian
Dimension: \(\mu_j \in \mathbb{R}^D\) (a vector of \(D\) values)
Interpretation: The “typical” point of component \(j\)



3. The Covariance Matrices \(\Sigma_j\)

What they are: Describes the shape, orientation, and dispersion of each Gaussian
Properties:

\(D \times D\) matrix (square)
Symmetric: \(\Sigma_j = \Sigma_j^T\)
Positive definite (all eigenvalues > 0)

Geometric interpretation:

The diagonal: variances in each direction
Off-diagonal elements: covariances (correlations between dimensions)


The set of parameters: \(\theta = \{\pi_j, \mu_j, \Sigma_j\}_{j=1}^c\)

title: Exam questions
text:
4. Calculation and Interpretation

How to Calculate the Density?
For a point \(x\), the density according to the GMM is:

For each component \(j\):

Calculate \(\mathcal{N}(x|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)\): the “height” of Gaussian \(j\) at point \(x\)
Multiply by \(\pi_j\): weight by the importance of the component

Sum over all components:

\(f(x) = \pi_1 \times \text{height}_1 + \pi_2 \times \text{height}_2 + ... + \pi_c \times \text{height}_c\)




Visual Interpretation
Imagine a mountain landscape: * Each Gaussian is a mountain * \(\mu_j\) is the mountain peak * \(\Sigma_j\) describes how the mountain spreads (is it round? elongated?) * \(\pi_j\) is the relative height of the mountain * \(f(x)\) is the total altitude at position \(x\)

title: Exam questions
section: 5. Latent Variables: The Key to Interpretation
text:
5. Latent Variables: The Key to Interpretation

The Problem of Missing Labels
In a real problem, we don’t know which component generated each point. This missing information is what we call latent variable.
Let \(z_i\) be the latent variable for point \(x_i\): * \(z_i = j\) means “\(x_i\) comes from component \(j\)” * We don’t observe the \(z_i\), only the \(x_i\)


Probabilistic Reformulation
With latent variables, the model becomes:

Prior probability: \(\mathbb{P}(z = j) = \pi_j\)
Conditional probability: \(\mathbb{P}(x|z = j) = \mathcal{N}(x|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)\)
Joint probability: \(\mathbb{P}(x, z = j) = \pi_j \mathcal{N}(x|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)\)
Marginal probability (what we observe): \(\mathbb{P}(x) = \sum_j \pi_j \mathcal{N}(x|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)\)

title: Exam questions
text:
6. Parameter Optimization: The EM Algorithm

The Challenge
We want to find the parameters \(\theta\) that maximize the likelihood of the observed data:
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^N f(x_i|\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^{c} \pi_j \mathcal{N}(x_i|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)
\]
The problem is the logarithm of a sum in the log-likelihood:
\[
\log \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log \left( \sum_{j=1}^{c} \pi_j \mathcal{N}(x_i|\mu_j, \Sigma_j) \right)
\]
Difficult to optimize directly!


The Solution: EM Algorithm (Expectation-Maximization)
EM solves this problem through an iterative two-step approach:





graph TD
    A[Random initialization] --> B[E-step: Responsibility calculation];
    B --> C[M-step: Parameter update];
    C --> D{Convergence?};
    D -- No --> B;
    D -- Yes --> E[Optimal parameters];







Step 0: Initialization
We start with initial parameters: * \(\pi_j^{(0)} = 1/c\) (equal weights) * \(\mu_j^{(0)}\) chosen randomly from the data * \(\Sigma_j^{(0)} = I\) (identity matrix)


E-step (Expectation): Responsibility Calculation
This is the crucial step! We calculate for each point \(x_i\) and each component \(j\):
\[
\gamma_{ij} = \mathbb{P}(z_i = j | x_i, \theta) = \frac{\pi_j \mathcal{N}(x_i|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^c \pi_k \mathcal{N}(x_i|\mu_k, \Sigma_k)}
\]
Intuitive interpretation: \(\gamma_{ij}\) answers the question: “If I see point \(x_i\), what’s the probability it came from component \(j\)?”
Important property: \(\sum_{j=1}^c \gamma_{ij} = 1\) for all \(i\). Each point is “distributed” among the components.


M-step (Maximization): Parameter Update
Now we use the responsibilities to update the parameters:

New weights:
\[
\pi_j^{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij}
\]
Interpretation: The average proportion of responsibility assigned to component \(j\).
New means:
\[
\mu_j^{\text{new}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij} x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij}}
\]
Interpretation: The weighted average of all points, with \(\gamma_{ij}\) as weights.
New covariances:
\[
\Sigma_j^{\text{new}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij} (x_i - \mu_j^{\text{new}})(x_i - \mu_j^{\text{new}})^T}{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij}}
\]
Interpretation: The weighted covariance around the new mean.



Iteration until Convergence
We repeat the E and M steps until: * Parameters change very little * Likelihood no longer improves significantly

title: Exam questions
section: 7. Why Does It Work? The Intuition
text:
7. Why Does It Work? The Intuition

The Teacher and Students Analogy
Imagine a teacher who wants to understand two groups of students in their class (the “math whizzes” and the “literary types”), but doesn’t know who belongs to which group.

Initialization: The teacher makes an initial hypothesis about each group’s characteristics.
E-step: For each student, the teacher estimates the probability they’re a “math whiz” or “literary type” based on current grades.
M-step: The teacher redefines what a “math whiz” and “literary type” are by looking at students probably in each group.
Repetition: With these new definitions, they reassess probabilities, and so on.



The Magic of “Soft” Responsibilities
Unlike K-means which says “this student is either a math whiz or literary type”, EM says “this student might be 70% math whiz and 30% literary type”. This soft assignment allows for more nuanced modeling.

title: Exam questions
text:
8. Concrete Step-by-Step Example

Data: Animal Sizes
Suppose we measure animals and get these sizes (in cm): [10, 12, 14, 90, 95, 100]
There appear to be two groups: small animals (10-14 cm) and large animals (90-100 cm).


Step-by-Step with EM

Initialization:

\(c = 2\) (two components)
\(\pi_1 = \pi_2 = 0.5\)
\(\mu_1 = 12\), \(\mu_2 = 95\) (chosen approximately)
\(\Sigma_1 = \Sigma_2 = 1\) (unit variance)

First E-step:

For \(x = 10\): \(\gamma_{11} \approx 0.95\), \(\gamma_{12} \approx 0.05\)
For \(x = 95\): \(\gamma_{21} \approx 0.01\), \(\gamma_{22} \approx 0.99\)

First M-step:

\(\pi_1^{\text{new}} = (0.95+0.8+0.6+0.05+0.01+0.01)/6 \approx 0.40\)
\(\pi_2^{\text{new}} \approx 0.60\)
\(\mu_1^{\text{new}} \approx 12.5\), \(\mu_2^{\text{new}} \approx 94.5\)

Subsequent iterations: Parameters refine with each iteration.

title: Exam questions
text:
9. Important Practical Aspects

Choosing the Number of Components (\(c\))
How to decide how many Gaussians to use?
Methods: 1. Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC): Penalizes overly complex models
\[
   \text{BIC} = -2 \log \mathcal{L} + k \log N
   \]
where \(k\) is the number of parameters, \(N\) the number of points.

Cross-validation
Visual inspection (when possible in 2D/3D)



Initialization Problems
EM converges to a local optimum. Poor initialization gives poor results.
Solutions: * Multiple trials with different initializations * Use K-means for smart initialization * K-means++ for better dispersion of initial centers


Types of Covariance Matrices

Spherical: \(\Sigma = \sigma^2 I\) (all directions equal)
Diagonal: \(\Sigma = \text{diag}(\sigma_1^2, ..., \sigma_D^2)\) (independent directions)
Full: \(\Sigma\) complete (with correlations)

Choice: The more constrained the matrix, the fewer parameters, but the less flexible the model.

title: Exam questions
text:
10. Concrete Applications

1. Image Segmentation
Separate foreground from background in a photo.


2. Speech Recognition
Model different frequency components of voice.


3. Anomaly Detection
Points with low density under the GMM are potentially anomalies.


4. Data Compression
Represent a complex distribution with a few Gaussians.

title: Exam questions
text:
Conclusion: The Power of GMM
The Gaussian Mixture Model is a remarkably flexible tool that:

Models complexity: Can approximate almost any distribution
Provides uncertainties: Gives probabilities, not just binary decisions
Interprets well: Each parameter has intuitive meaning
Optimizes efficiently: Thanks to the EM algorithm

The key concept to remember is that of responsibility (\(\gamma_{ij}\)): it’s what transforms a difficult optimization problem into an elegant iterative procedure where each point partially participates in learning all components.
As statistician George Box said: “All models are wrong, but some are useful.” The GMM is certainly one of the most useful for modeling the complexity of the real world.

section: Introduction: The Problem of Incomplete Data
text:
Introduction: The Problem of Incomplete Data
Imagine you inherit several bags of mixed coins. Some coins are gold, others silver, but they’re all in the same bag. Your mission: determine the average composition of gold and silver coins without being able to physically separate them.
This is exactly the type of problem solved by the EM algorithm (Expectation-Maximization), and the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) is its most famous application.

title: Exam questions
text:
1. What is the EM Algorithm?

Simple Definition
The EM algorithm is an intelligent iterative method for finding optimal parameters of a statistical model when some information is missing.
Medical analogy: Imagine a doctor who wants to diagnose two rare diseases. The symptoms overlap, and they’re never 100% sure of the disease. The EM algorithm would be their method for:

Estimating the probability of each disease for each patient (E-step)
Updating the description of diseases based on these probabilities (M-step)
Repeating until diagnosis stabilizes



The Fundamental Problem Solved by EM
In many real problems, we have:

Observed data: What we measure
Missing/latent data: What we don’t see but influences observations

The challenge: How to estimate a model when a crucial part of information is hidden?

section: 3. The Heart of the Algorithm: The Concept of Responsibility
text:
3. The Heart of the Algorithm: The Concept of Responsibility

Intuitive Definition
The responsibility (denoted \(\gamma_{ij}\)) is the probability that a data point \(x_i\) was generated by component \(j\) of the mixture.
Social analogy: Imagine a party with several conversation groups. The responsibility \(\gamma_{ij}\) answers the question: “If I look at a person \(x_i\), what’s the probability they belong to conversation group \(j\)?”


Mathematical Definition
Formally, for a GMM with parameters \(\theta = \{\pi_j, \mu_j, \Sigma_j\}\):
\[
\gamma_{ij} = \frac{\pi_j \cdot \mathcal{N}(x_i|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^c \pi_k \cdot \mathcal{N}(x_i|\mu_k, \Sigma_k)}
\]
Where:

\(\pi_j\) is the weight (importance) of component \(j\)
\(\mathcal{N}(x_i|\mu_j, \Sigma_j)\) is the “likelihood” that \(x_i\) came from component \(j\)
The denominator ensures that \(\sum_j \gamma_{ij} = 1\) (sum of probabilities equals 1)



Essential Properties of Responsibilities

Normalization: For each point \(i\), \(\sum_{j=1}^c \gamma_{ij} = 1\)

Each point is “distributed” among all components

Continuity: \(\gamma_{ij} \in [0, 1]\) (a true probability)

Unlike K-means which gives 0 or 1

Interpretation as weights: The closer \(\gamma_{ij}\) is to 1, the more point \(i\) “belongs” to component \(j\)

title: Exam questions
section: 4. How Does the EM Algorithm Work for GMM?
text:
4. How Does the EM Algorithm Work for GMM?

The Two-Step Principle
The EM algorithm works like a dialogue between two experts:

The assignment expert (E-step): “Given current parameters, what are the membership probabilities?”
The parameter expert (M-step): “Given these probabilities, what are the best parameters?”



Step by Step

Step 0: Initialization
We start with an initial parameter estimate. This is like making an initial hypothesis about the groups.
Common initialization strategies:

Initialize weights uniformly: \(\pi_j^{(0)} = 1/c\)
Choose means \(\mu_j^{(0)}\) randomly from the data
Initialize covariances to identity matrix: \(\Sigma_j^{(0)} = I\)



E-step (Expectation): Responsibility Calculation
This is the “Expectation” step. For each point \(x_i\) and each component \(j\):

Calculate affinity: How much does \(x_i\) resemble component \(j\)?
\[
\text{affinity} = \pi_j \times \text{height of Gaussian } j \text{ at point } x_i
\]
Normalize: Transform these affinities into probabilities

Concrete example: For a point exactly between two Gaussians with equal weights:

\(\gamma_{i1} = 0.5\) (50% chance of being in group 1)
\(\gamma_{i2} = 0.5\) (50% chance of being in group 2)



M-step (Maximization): Parameter Update
Now we use responsibilities as weights to recalculate parameters:

New means (\(\mu_j\)):
\[
\mu_j^{\text{new}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij} \cdot x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij}}
\]
Interpretation: The weighted average of all points, where each point \(x_i\) is weighted by its responsibility \(\gamma_{ij}\).
New covariances (\(\Sigma_j\)):
\[
\Sigma_j^{\text{new}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij} \cdot (x_i - \mu_j^{\text{new}})(x_i - \mu_j^{\text{new}})^T}{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij}}
\]
Interpretation: How points are dispersed around the new mean, weighted by their responsibilities.
New weights (\(\pi_j\)):
\[
\pi_j^{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ij}
\]
Interpretation: The average proportion of responsibility assigned to component \(j\).



Iteration until Convergence
We repeat E → M → E → M until:

Parameters hardly change
Responsibilities stabilize
Data likelihood no longer increases

title: Exam questions
text:
5. Visualization of the EM Process

First Cycle
Initial state:

2 misplaced Gaussians
Blurry boundaries

After E-step:

Each point receives responsibilities (ex: [0.7, 0.3], [0.2, 0.8], etc.)
Points at centers have more extreme responsibilities
Points at boundaries have balanced responsibilities

After M-step:

Gaussians move toward points that “belong” to them
They change shape to better fit “their” points
Weights adjust according to proportion of assigned points



Progressive Convergence
At each iteration:

Responsibilities become more certain (close to 0 or 1)
Gaussians separate better
The model improves at explaining data

title: Exam questions
text:
6. Why Are Responsibilities So Important?

They Transform a Difficult Problem into a Simple One
Without responsibilities (difficult problem):

Log-likelihood: \(\sum_i \log(\sum_j ...)\)
Impossible to optimize directly

With responsibilities (simple problem):

We treat each point as partially belonging to all clusters
Optimization becomes a weighted average



They Enable “Soft” Assignment
Unlike K-means which says “this point is IN or OUT of the cluster”, EM says “this point is X% in cluster A and Y% in cluster B”. This nuance is crucial for:

Border points: A point between two clusters will have balanced responsibilities
Uncertainty: We know when we’re not sure
Robustness: Less sensitive to random initializations

section: 7. Concrete Example: Separating Two Animal Species
text:
7. Concrete Example: Separating Two Animal Species

Data
We measure animal height and weight. Visually, we see two groups but with overlap.


EM Application
Iteration 1:

A medium-sized animal: \(\gamma = [0.6, 0.4]\) (rather group 1)
Gaussians are poorly adjusted

Iteration 5:

Same animal: \(\gamma = [0.8, 0.2]\) (more confident)
Gaussians have separated

Iteration 10 (convergence):

The animal: \(\gamma = [0.95, 0.05]\) (very confident)
Gaussians are well separated and adjusted



Biological Interpretation
Responsibilities tell us:

Which animals are potential hybrids (balanced responsibilities)
Which animals are typical representatives of their species (extreme responsibilities)
Where the overlap zones between species are

title: Exam questions
text:
8. The Deep EM-GMM Relationship

EM as the “Engine” of GMM
GMM defines the structure: “data comes from several Gaussians” The EM algorithm provides the method: “how to find these Gaussians”


The Virtuous Cycle
EM cycle:

Better parameters → More precise responsibilities
More precise responsibilities → Even better parameters
Repeat until perfection



Difference from K-means
K-means is like EM with a binary vision:

K-means: “This point is IN or OUT of the cluster”
EM: “This point is X% in cluster A, Y% in B, …”

section: 9. Practical Applications of EM with GMM
text:
9. Practical Applications of EM with GMM

1. Speech Recognition

Each phoneme is modeled by a GMM
EM finds parameters for each phoneme
Responsibilities help identify transitions between phonemes



2. Image Segmentation

Different image regions = different components
EM segments image into coherent regions
Responsibilities give fuzzy boundaries (more realistic)



3. Fraud Detection

Normal behaviors = one component
Abnormal behaviors = another component
Responsibilities indicate degree of abnormality

title: Exam questions
text:
10. Limitations and Solutions

Initialization Problem
EM converges to a local optimum. Poor initialization gives poor results.
Solution: Multiple trials with different initializations, or use K-means to initialize.


Choosing Number of Components
EM doesn’t tell us how many components to use.
Solution: Use BIC criterion that penalizes overly complex models.


Computational Complexity
Calculating all responsibilities can be costly for large datasets.
Solution: Approximations, or mini-batch processing.

title: Exam questions
section: Conclusion: The Elegance of the EM Approach
text:
Conclusion: The Elegance of the EM Approach
The EM algorithm, with its central concept of responsibility, elegantly solves a seemingly unsolvable problem: how to learn from a mixture when you can’t separate the ingredients.
The beauty of this approach lies in its reflexivity:

We use parameters to estimate responsibilities
We use responsibilities to improve parameters
Each cycle improves both

GMM is just one application of the EM algorithm, but it’s a particularly elegant application that shows the full power of the responsibility concept. By allowing points to partially belong to multiple clusters, EM captures the nuance and uncertainty inherent in real data.
As statistician George Box said: “All models are wrong, but some are useful.” The EM-GMM duo is not only useful, but also remarkably intuitive once you understand the concept of responsibility.

Question
Explain how the model of Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) relate to conditional model for classification.

title: Exam questions
section: Introduction to Conditional Modeling in Classification
text:
Introduction to Conditional Modeling in Classification
In supervised classification problems, we aim to predict the class label \(y\) of an observation \(x\).
A fundamental approach involves modeling the conditional probability \(P(y|x)\), i.e., the probability that an observation \(x\) belongs to a given class \(y\).

title: Exam questions
text:
Bayesian Framework for Classification

Bayes’ Rule for Optimal Decision
According to Bayes’ theorem, the posterior probability that an observation \(x\) belongs to class \(k\) is:
\[
P(C = k | x) = \frac{P(x | C = k) \cdot P(C = k)}{P(x)}
\]
Where: - \(P(C = k)\) is the prior probability of class \(k\) - \(P(x | C = k)\) is the likelihood of \(x\) given class \(k\) - \(P(x)\) is the marginal probability of \(x\) (constant for all classes)
The optimal decision rule (minimizing the error rate) consists of assigning \(x\) to the class \(k\) that maximizes the posterior probability:
\[
\delta(x) = \arg\max_k P(C = k | x)
\]
Since \(P(x)\) is constant, this rule is equivalent to:
\[
\delta(x) = \arg\max_k \left[ P(x | C = k) \cdot P(C = k) \right]
\]

title: Exam questions
section: LDA as a Conditional Generative Model
text:
LDA as a Conditional Generative Model

Fundamental Assumptions of LDA
Linear Discriminant Analysis is based on three clear assumptions:

Gaussian distribution per class: Each class follows a multivariate normal distribution
\[
P(x | C = k) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \Sigma)
\]
Common covariance matrix: All classes share the same covariance matrix \(\Sigma\)
Prior probabilities: Classes have prior probabilities \(P(C = k)\) (often estimated by sample proportions)



Explicit Formulation of the LDA Model
Under these assumptions, the probability density for class \(k\) is written as:
\[
P(x | C = k) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2} |\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (x - \mu_k)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu_k) \right)
\]
Where \(D\) is the data dimension, \(\mu_k\) is the mean vector of class \(k\), and \(\Sigma\) is the common covariance matrix.

title: Exam questions
section: From Conditional Modeling to Linear Discriminant Function
text:
From Conditional Modeling to Linear Discriminant Function

Derivation of the Decision Function
By applying the Bayesian decision rule and taking the logarithm (which preserves maxima), we obtain:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta(x) &= \arg\max_k \left[ \ln P(x | C = k) + \ln P(C = k) \right] \\
&= \arg\max_k \left[ -\frac{1}{2} (x - \mu_k)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu_k) + \ln P(C = k) + \text{constant} \right]
\end{aligned}
\]
By expanding the quadratic term and eliminating terms independent of \(k\), we obtain the linear discriminant function:
\[
\delta(x) = \arg\max_k \left[ x^T \Sigma^{-1} \mu_k - \frac{1}{2} \mu_k^T \Sigma^{-1} \mu_k + \ln P(C = k) \right]
\]


Explicit Form of the Decision Boundary
The discriminant function for class \(k\) can be written as a linear function in \(x\):
\[
g_k(x) = w_k^T x + b_k
\]
Where: - \(w_k = \Sigma^{-1} \mu_k\) is the weight vector for class \(k\) - \(b_k = -\frac{1}{2} \mu_k^T \Sigma^{-1} \mu_k + \ln P(C = k)\) is the bias for class \(k\)
The decision boundary between two classes \(k\) and \(l\) is then linear:
\[
\{x : g_k(x) = g_l(x)\} \quad \Rightarrow \quad (w_k - w_l)^T x + (b_k - b_l) = 0
\]

title: Exam questions
section: Geometric Interpretation and Link with Fisher’s Criterion
text:
Geometric Interpretation and Link with Fisher’s Criterion

Optimal Projection for Discrimination
LDA seeks the projection direction \(a\) that maximizes the relative separation between classes.
Fisher’s criterion, which maximizes:
\[
J(a) = \frac{a^T \Sigma_b a}{a^T \Sigma_w a}
\]
corresponds exactly to finding the direction that maximizes the ratio between: - \(\Sigma_b\): between-class dispersion (to maximize) - \(\Sigma_w\): within-class dispersion (to minimize)


Equivalence with the Probabilistic Approach
When the prior probabilities are equal (\(P(C = k) = 1/M\)), the LDA solution via Fisher’s criterion is equivalent to the solution obtained by the Gaussian modeling approach with common covariance.
The optimal direction \(a\) is given by the first eigenvector of \(\Sigma_w^{-1} \Sigma_b\), which in the two-class case reduces to:
\[
a \propto \Sigma^{-1} (\mu_1 - \mu_2)
\]
Exactly the same expression as in the Bayesian approach!

title: Exam questions
text:
Model Parameter Estimation

Maximum Likelihood Approach
From a training sample \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N\), LDA parameters are naturally estimated:

Class means: \(\hat{\mu}_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_{i: y_i = k} x_i\)
Common covariance matrix: \(\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N - M} \sum_{k=1}^M \sum_{i: y_i = k} (x_i - \hat{\mu}_k)(x_i - \hat{\mu}_k)^T\)
Prior probabilities: \(\hat{P}(C = k) = \frac{N_k}{N}\)

These estimators are consistent and asymptotically efficient under the model assumptions.

title: Exam questions
section: Advantages of the Conditional Interpretation of LDA
text:
Advantages of the Conditional Interpretation of LDA

1. Solid Probabilistic Foundations
Unlike a simple search for discriminant directions, LDA provides a complete generative model that allows: - Generating synthetic data for each class - Calculating well-calibrated posterior probabilities - Incorporating prior knowledge about classes


2. Ability to Handle Imbalanced Classes
By using prior probabilities \(P(C = k)\), LDA can naturally account for unequal class frequencies.


3. Extension to Multi-Class Classification
The probabilistic framework naturally extends to \(M > 2\) classes, whereas Fisher’s criterion requires generalizations.


4. Interpretation in Terms of Likelihood Ratio
The decision between two classes \(k\) and \(l\) can be expressed as:
\[
\log \frac{P(C = k | x)}{P(C = l | x)} = (w_k - w_l)^T x + (b_k - b_l)
\]
This corresponds to a likelihood ratio test with a threshold adapted to prior probabilities.

title: Exam questions
text:
Limitations and Extensions

Restrictive Common Covariance Assumption
The main limitation of LDA is the assumption that all classes share the same covariance matrix \(\Sigma\).
When this assumption is not verified, we use: - QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis): allows different covariances per class, leading to quadratic boundaries - Regularizations: regularized versions of LDA for high-dimensional data


Modern Extensions

Flexible LDA: uses kernels to capture non-linearities
Sparse LDA: introduces sparsity constraints for variable selection
Robust LDA: versions resistant to outliers

title: Exam questions
text:
Concrete Example: Iris Flower Classification
Consider the Iris dataset with 3 flower species.
LDA models each species by a Gaussian distribution in the feature space (petal/sepal length and width).
For a new flower measurement \(x\), LDA calculates: 1. The likelihood \(P(x | \text{setosa})\), \(P(x | \text{versicolor})\), \(P(x | \text{virginica})\) 2. The posterior probabilities via Bayes’ rule 3. Assigns the species with the maximum posterior probability
The boundary between species appears linear in the feature space, due to the common covariance assumption.

title: Exam questions
text:
Conclusion
Linear Discriminant Analysis is fundamentally a conditional model for classification that:

Explicitly models \(P(x | C = k)\) as Gaussians with common covariance
Uses Bayes’ rule to calculate \(P(C = k | x)\) and make decisions
Reduces to linear discriminant functions thanks to its simplifying assumptions
Is equivalent to Fisher’s criterion under the assumption of balanced classes

This dual perspective - both as a probabilistic generative model and as a discriminant projection method - explains the power and enduring popularity of LDA in statistical learning.
LDA perfectly illustrates how well-chosen probabilistic assumptions can lead to simple and interpretable algorithms while remaining theoretically grounded and practically effective.

title: Exam questions
text:
Question
Explain the method of Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) including assumptions, calculation, and interpretation of the technique.
How is this technique used for classification?

title: Exam questions
text:
What is Linear Discriminant Analysis?
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a supervised statistical method that serves two main functions: classification and dimensionality reduction.
It aims to find linear combinations of the original variables that best separate different predefined classes.

title: Exam questions
text:
Fundamental Assumptions of LDA
For LDA to function optimally, it relies on several key assumptions:

Gaussian Distribution
Each class is assumed to follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Formally, for each class \(k\), observations are drawn from:
\[
P(x | C = k) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \Sigma)
\]
where \(\mu_k\) is the mean vector of class \(k\) and \(\Sigma\) is the covariance matrix.


Homoscedasticity (Common Covariance)
All classes share the same covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). This assumption is crucial as it guarantees that decision boundaries will be linear.


Independent Observations
Observations are sampled independently and identically distributed within each class.


Class Separability
Class centers (\(\mu_k\)) must be sufficiently distinct relative to within-class dispersion.

title: Exam questions
text:
Calculation and Methodology

Notations and Definitions
Consider a problem with \(K\) classes:

\(N_k\): number of observations in class \(k\)
\(N\): total number of observations, with \(N = \sum_{k=1}^K N_k\)
\(\mu_k\): mean vector of class \(k\) (dimension \(D\))
\(\mu\): global mean vector of all observations



Dispersion Matrices

Within-Class Scatter Matrix
This matrix measures variability within each class:
\[
\Sigma_w = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{x_i \in \text{class } k} (x_i - \mu_k)(x_i - \mu_k)^T
\]


Between-Class Scatter Matrix
This matrix measures dispersion between centers of different classes:
\[
\Sigma_b = \sum_{k=1}^K N_k (\mu_k - \mu)(\mu_k - \mu)^T
\]



Fisher’s Criterion
LDA’s objective is to find a projection vector \(a\) that maximizes the relative separation between classes.
Fisher’s criterion formalizes this objective:
\[
J(a) = \frac{a^T \Sigma_b a}{a^T \Sigma_w a}
\]
The numerator \(a^T \Sigma_b a\) represents the projected between-class dispersion (to maximize), while the denominator \(a^T \Sigma_w a\) represents the projected within-class dispersion (to minimize).


Optimization Solution
Maximizing \(J(a)\) reduces to solving a generalized eigenvalue problem:
\[
\Sigma_b a = \lambda \Sigma_w a
\]
In practice, we compute the eigenvectors of \(\Sigma_w^{-1} \Sigma_b\) (provided \(\Sigma_w\) is invertible).


Detailed Calculation Steps
Step 1: Calculate Descriptive Statistics

Class means: \(\hat{\mu}_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_{i: y_i = k} x_i\)
Global mean: \(\hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N x_i\)

Step 2: Calculate Dispersion Matrices

Within-class matrix: \(\hat{\Sigma}_w = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i: y_i = k} (x_i - \hat{\mu}_k)(x_i - \hat{\mu}_k)^T\)
Between-class matrix: \(\hat{\Sigma}_b = \sum_{k=1}^K N_k (\hat{\mu}_k - \hat{\mu})(\hat{\mu}_k - \hat{\mu})^T\)

Step 3: Solve Eigenvalue Problem

Compute matrix \(\hat{\Sigma}_w^{-1} \hat{\Sigma}_b\)
Extract eigenvectors corresponding to the largest eigenvalues

Step 4: Form Discriminant Space

Sort eigenvectors by descending eigenvalues
Form projection matrix \(W = [a_1, a_2, ..., a_{K-1}]\) (at most \(K-1\) non-zero directions)

Step 5: Project Data
\[
Y = XW
\]
where \(Y\) represents the data projected into the new discriminant space.

title: Exam questions
text:
Interpretation of Results

Discriminant Dimensions
Each eigenvector \(a_i\) corresponds to a direction in the original space along which class separation is maximal.
The associated eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) measures the discriminant power of this direction.


Explained Separation Percentage
We can evaluate the relative importance of each discriminant dimension:
\[
\text{Proportion}_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{K-1} \lambda_j} \times 100\%
\]


Coefficient Significance
The coefficients of vector \(a_i\) indicate the relative importance of each original variable in discrimination.
A high absolute coefficient means the variable strongly contributes to class separation along that direction.


Visualization
By projecting the data onto the first two discriminant dimensions, we obtain a 2D visualization that allows appreciating the separation between classes.

title: Exam questions
text:
Use for Classification

Probabilistic Modeling Approach
LDA can be interpreted as a generative model where each class is modeled by a normal distribution:
\[
P(x | C = k) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mu_k)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu_k)\right)
\]


Probability Estimation

Prior Probabilities
Estimated by observed proportions in the sample:
\[
\hat{P}(C = k) = \frac{N_k}{N}
\]


Bayes’ Rule for Classification
The probability that an observation \(x\) belongs to class \(k\) is given by:
\[
P(C = k | x) = \frac{P(x | C = k) P(C = k)}{\sum_{l=1}^K P(x | C = l) P(C = l)}
\]



Linear Discriminant Functions
For each class \(k\), we define a linear function:
\[
g_k(x) = w_k^T x + b_k
\]
with: - \(w_k = \Sigma^{-1} \mu_k\) - \(b_k = -\frac{1}{2} \mu_k^T \Sigma^{-1} \mu_k + \ln P(C = k)\)


Decision Rule
We assign \(x\) to the class that maximizes the discriminant function:
\[
\hat{y} = \arg\max_{k} g_k(x)
\]
This is equivalent to choosing the class with the highest posterior probability \(P(C = k | x)\).


Decision Boundaries
The boundary between two classes \(k\) and \(l\) is linear:
\[
\{x : g_k(x) = g_l(x)\} \quad \Rightarrow \quad (w_k - w_l)^T x + (b_k - b_l) = 0
\]
This linearity is a direct consequence of the common covariance assumption.


Classification Process for a New Observation
To classify a new observation \(x_{\text{new}}\):

Compute scores: Evaluate \(g_k(x_{\text{new}})\) for each class \(k\)
Decision: Assign to the class with the highest score
Probabilistic option: Calculate posterior probabilities \(P(C = k | x_{\text{new}})\) for a probabilistic decision



Parameter Estimation
From a training sample \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N\):

Class means: \(\hat{\mu}_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_{i: y_i = k} x_i\)
Common covariance: \(\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N-K} \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i: y_i = k} (x_i - \hat{\mu}_k)(x_i - \hat{\mu}_k)^T\)
Prior probabilities: \(\hat{P}(C = k) = \frac{N_k}{N}\)

title: Exam questions
text:
Advantages and Limitations

Advantages

Solid theoretical foundations based on Bayesian theory and Fisher’s criterion
Computational efficiency: analytical solution without iterative optimization
Interpretability: discriminant directions have clear geometric meaning
Dual functionality: integrated dimensionality reduction and classification
Robustness to slight violations of normality



Limitations

Sensitivity to outliers affecting mean and covariance estimates
Common covariance assumption sometimes unrealistic in practice
Linearity: cannot capture non-linear relationships between variables
Normality requirement: degraded performance with strongly non-Gaussian distributions



Alternatives and Extensions

QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis): relaxes common covariance assumption, giving quadratic boundaries
Regularized LDA: introduces regularization for high-dimensional problems
Flexible Discriminant Analysis: uses basis functions to capture non-linear relationships
Support Vector Machines (SVM): alternative approach for linear and non-linear classification

title: Exam questions
text:
Concrete Example: Iris Flower Classification

Problem Context
The Iris dataset contains 3 flower species with 4 morphological characteristics: - Sepal length and width - Petal length and width


LDA Application
Step 1: Parameter estimation
Calculate means for each species and common covariance matrix.
Step 2: Discriminant direction calculation
Solve eigenvalue problem to obtain 2 directions (since \(K-1=2\)).
Step 3: Projection and visualization
Reduce data to 2 dimensions, revealing good separation between species.
Step 4: Classification
Construct discriminant functions allowing classification of new flowers with high accuracy (>95%).

title: Exam questions
text:
Conclusion
Linear Discriminant Analysis is an elegant and powerful method that combines several approaches:

A geometric perspective seeking optimal projection directions
A probabilistic modeling based on normal distributions
An optimal Bayesian decision rule under its assumptions

Its versatility (classification and dimensionality reduction) and high interpretability make it a valuable tool in exploratory data analysis and predictive modeling.
However, its successful application depends on the reasonable fulfillment of its underlying assumptions.
When these assumptions hold, LDA provides an efficient, interpretable, and theoretically grounded solution to classification and group separation problems.

title: Exam questions
text:
Question
Explain in detail the principal component analysis (PCA) method, including the assumptions, calculation and interpretation of this technique.

title: Exam questions
text:
Introduction and Objectives
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a dimensionality reduction method that transforms a set of potentially correlated variables into a set of linearly uncorrelated variables called principal components.

Main Objectives

Reduce data dimensionality while preserving maximum information
Identify directions of greatest variance in the data
Decorate variables
Visualize multidimensional data

title: Exam questions
text:
Fundamental Assumptions

Statistical Assumptions

Linearity: Relationships between variables are linear
Normal Distribution: Data approximately follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution
\[
X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\overline{\mathbf{x}}, \Sigma)
\]
Importance of Variance: Variance is an appropriate measure of the information contained in the data
Orthogonality: Principal components are orthogonal to each other



Data Prerequisites

Data must be centered (zero mean)
Variable scales must be comparable (normalization recommended)
No significant missing values

title: Exam questions
text:
Calculation of Principal Components

Step 1: Data Preparation
Centering: Subtract the mean of each variable
\[
\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{centered}} = \mathbf{x}_i - \overline{\mathbf{x}}, \quad \text{where} \quad \overline{\mathbf{x}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{x}_i
\]
Normalization (optional but recommended): Divide by the standard deviation
\[
\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{norm}} = \frac{\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{centered}}}{\sigma}, \quad \text{where} \quad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \overline{x})^2}
\]


Step 2: Calculation of the Covariance Matrix
For \(N\) observations with \(D\) variables, the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) is:
\[
\Sigma = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\mathbf{x}_i - \overline{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_i - \overline{\mathbf{x}})^\top
\]
Properties of \(\Sigma\):

Symmetric: \(\Sigma = \Sigma^\top\)
Positive semi-definite: \(\mathbf{v}^\top \Sigma \mathbf{v} \geq 0\) for all \(\mathbf{v}\)
Diagonal elements: variances of variables
Off-diagonal elements: covariances between variables



Step 3: Eigenvalue Decomposition
We seek the eigenpairs \((\lambda_d, \mathbf{u}_d)\) such that:
\[
\Sigma \mathbf{u}_d = \lambda_d \mathbf{u}_d, \quad d = 1, \dots, D
\]
Order of eigenvalues: \(\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \dots \geq \lambda_D \geq 0\)
Matrix of eigenvectors: \(\mathbf{U} = [\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2, \dots, \mathbf{u}_D]\)

Fundamental Relation: Eigenvalue = Variance

Mathematical Demonstration
Step 1: Projected variance
Let \(\mathbf{u}\) be a unit vector. The projection of an observation \(\mathbf{x}_i\) onto \(\mathbf{u}\) is:
\[
p_i = \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{x}_i
\]
Step 2: Variance calculation
The mean of projections (for centered data) is zero:
\[
\bar{p} = \mathbf{u}^\top \bar{\mathbf{x}} = 0
\]
The variance of projections is therefore:
\[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{u}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (p_i)^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)^2
\]
Step 3: Matrix formulation
\[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{u}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^\top \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^\top \right) \mathbf{u}
\]
But \(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^\top = \Sigma\)
So:
\[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{u}^\top \Sigma \mathbf{u}
\]
Step 4: Constrained maximization
We seek \(\mathbf{u}_1\) maximizing \(\mathbf{u}^\top \Sigma \mathbf{u}\) under \(\|\mathbf{u}\| = 1\).
Lagrangian:
\[
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \lambda) = \mathbf{u}^\top \Sigma \mathbf{u} - \lambda(\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u} - 1)
\]






NoneConcise explanation of the role of \(\lambda\)





In PCA, we maximize \(\mathbf{u}^T\Sigma\mathbf{u}\) under the constraint \(\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{u} = 1\).
The \(\lambda\) appears naturally when using the method of Lagrange multipliers to solve this constrained optimization problem.
The Lagrange function is written: \[
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \lambda) = \mathbf{u}^T\Sigma\mathbf{u} - \lambda(\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{u} - 1)
\]
The term \(-\lambda(\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{u} - 1)\) allows us to incorporate the constraint directly into the objective function. The multiplier \(\lambda\) serves as a penalty parameter that ensures the solution respects the unit norm constraint.
Thus, \(\lambda\) is essentially a mathematical artifact that allows us to transform a constrained optimization problem into an equivalent unconstrained problem.



Optimality condition:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{u}} = 2\Sigma \mathbf{u} - 2\lambda \mathbf{u} = 0
\]
That is:
\[
\Sigma \mathbf{u} = \lambda \mathbf{u}
\]
Step 5: Interpretation
For an eigenvector \(\mathbf{u}_d\) satisfying \(\Sigma \mathbf{u}_d = \lambda_d \mathbf{u}_d\):
\[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{u}_d) = \mathbf{u}_d^\top \Sigma \mathbf{u}_d = \mathbf{u}_d^\top (\lambda_d \mathbf{u}_d) = \lambda_d \mathbf{u}_d^\top \mathbf{u}_d = \lambda_d
\]
Because \(\mathbf{u}_d^\top \mathbf{u}_d = \|\mathbf{u}_d\|^2 = 1\).


Conclusion
Each eigenvalue \(\lambda_d\) is exactly the variance of the data projected onto the corresponding eigenvector \(\mathbf{u}_d\).



Order of Components
We order by decreasing eigenvalues:
\[
\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \dots \geq \lambda_D \geq 0
\]
Thus:

\(\mathbf{u}_1\): direction of maximum variance
\(\mathbf{u}_2\): orthogonal direction of remaining maximum variance




Step 4: Component Selection

Explained Variance Criterion

Total Variance

Represents all the information contained in the original data
This is the reference: 100% of available information

\[
\text{Total Variance} = \sum_{d=1}^D \lambda_d = \text{Tr}(\Sigma)
\]


Explained Variance

Quantifies the information captured by each principal component
Corresponds directly to the eigenvalues \(\lambda_d\) of \(\Sigma\)
The larger \(\lambda_d\), the more variance the component explains
The explained variance by component \(d\) is: \[
\text{ExplainedVar}_d = \frac{\lambda_d}{\sum_{k=1}^{D} \lambda_k}
\]



Cumulative Variance

Progressive sum of explained variances component after component
Shows how much information is retained by selecting \(K\) components
Formula: \(\frac{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \cdots + \lambda_k}{\text{Total variance}}\)
Mathematically, the cumulative explained variance for \(K\) components is: \[
\text{CumulativeVar}_K = \frac{\sum_{d=1}^{K} \lambda_d}{\sum_{d=1}^{D} \lambda_d}
\]



Practical Usefulness

Choosing the number of components: Keep enough components to explain say 80-95% of total variance
Dimensionality reduction: Keep the essential information with fewer variables
Interpretation: Understand which components carry the most information

Visual example: If PC1 explains 60% and PC2 explains 20%, then with 2 components we capture 80% of total information.



Common Selection Rules

Elbow Method: Observe the “elbow” in the eigenvalue plot
Variance threshold: Keep enough components to explain 70-95% of total variance
Kaiser criterion: Keep components with eigenvalue > 1 (if data normalized)




Step 5: Data Projection
The projection of original data onto the first \(K\) components is:
\[
\mathbf{y}_i = \mathbf{U}_K^\top (\mathbf{x}_i - \overline{\mathbf{x}})
\]
where \(\mathbf{U}_K = [\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_K]\) contains the first \(K\) eigenvectors.

text:
Introduction to the Selection Problem
When we perform Principal Component Analysis, a crucial question arises: how many principal components should we keep? This choice represents a fundamental compromise between:

Dimensionality reduction (primary objective)
Information preservation (measured by explained variance)
Reconstruction quality of original data

title: Exam questions
text:
Main Selection Criteria

Based on Explained Variance

Cumulative Variance Threshold
The most common method is to keep enough components to explain a predefined percentage of total variance.
Calculation:
If we have \(D\) eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \dots \geq \lambda_D\), total variance is:
\[
\text{Total Variance} = \sum_{d=1}^D \lambda_d
\]
Variance explained by the first \(K\) components is:
\[
\text{Explained Variance}(K) = \sum_{d=1}^K \lambda_d
\]
Proportion of explained variance is:
\[
\text{PVE}(K) = \frac{\sum_{d=1}^K \lambda_d}{\sum_{d=1}^D \lambda_d}
\]
Practical rule: Choose \(K\) such that \(\text{PVE}(K) \geq \tau\), where \(\tau\) is typically between 70% and 95%.
Advantages:

Simple to understand and implement
Guarantees minimal information preservation
Standardized and reproducible

Disadvantages:

Choice of threshold \(\tau\) is arbitrary
Does not account for specific data structure




Eigenvalue Plot Analysis (Scree Plot)

Elbow Method
This visual method consists of plotting eigenvalues as a function of their order.
Procedure:

Plot \(\lambda_d\) versus \(d\) (for \(d = 1, 2, \dots, D\))
Identify the point where the curve forms an “elbow” (pronounced angle)
Keep components before the elbow

Interpretation:

Components before the elbow capture the main “signal”
Components after the elbow mainly capture “noise”

Advantages:

Intuitive and visual method
Takes into account relative eigenvalue decay

Disadvantages:

Subjective (different people may identify different elbows)
May be ambiguous for some eigenvalue distributions




Kaiser Rule (for Standardized Data)

Eigenvalue > 1 Threshold
When data is standardized (mean 0, variance 1), each original variable contributes 1 to total variance.
Rule: Keep components whose eigenvalue \(\lambda_d > 1\).
Justification: A component should explain at least as much variance as a single original variable.
Limitations:

Only applies to standardized data
Can be too conservative (too many components) or too lax (too few)




Method Based on Reconstruction Error

Quadratic Error Minimization
A more formal approach is to choose \(K\) that minimizes reconstruction error under a constraint.
Reconstruction error: For each observation \(\mathbf{x}_i\), reconstruction using \(K\) components is:
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = \overline{\mathbf{x}} + \sum_{d=1}^K (\mathbf{u}_d^\top (\mathbf{x}_i - \overline{\mathbf{x}})) \mathbf{u}_d
\]
Total quadratic error is:
\[
\mathcal{L}(K) = \sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{x}_i - \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i\|^2 = \sum_{d=K+1}^D \lambda_d
\]
Important relationship: Reconstruction error is exactly the sum of eigenvalues of excluded components.
Approach: Choose \(K\) such that \(\mathcal{L}(K) \leq \epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\) is an acceptable error threshold.

title: Exam questions
text:
Implications on Reconstruction

Exact Relationship between Number of Components and Quality

Eckart-Young Theorem
This fundamental theorem states that the rank-\(K\) approximation by PCA is optimal in the least squares sense.
Formalization: Let \(\mathbf{X}\) be the centered data matrix. Singular value decomposition (SVD) gives \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top\). The rank-\(K\) approximation:
\[
\mathbf{X}_K = \mathbf{U}_K \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_K \mathbf{V}_K^\top
\]
minimizes \(\|\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}_K\|_F^2\) among all rank-\(K\) matrices.
Implication: PCA provides the best rank-\(K\) approximation for centered data.



Dimension-Reconstruction Trade-off

Extreme Cases

\(K = D\): Perfect reconstruction

\(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = \mathbf{x}_i\) exactly
No dimensionality reduction
Conservation of 100% variance

\(K = 0\): Reconstruction by mean only

\(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = \overline{\mathbf{x}}\)
Maximum error: \(\mathcal{L}(0) = \sum_{d=1}^D \lambda_d\)
No information about individual variability




Typical Behavior
The relationship between \(K\) and reconstruction quality generally follows a law of diminishing returns:

First components significantly improve reconstruction
Improvements become progressively weaker
Beyond a certain point, gains are negligible




Impact on Applications

Visualization
For 2D or 3D visualization:

\(K = 2\) or \(3\): Allows direct visualization
Implication: Significant information loss if first two components don’t explain enough variance
Solution: Examine several component pairs if necessary



Denoising
PCA can separate signal and noise:

Signal: Captured by first components (high eigenvalues)
Noise: Captured by last components (low eigenvalues)
Choice of \(K\): Should be sufficient to capture signal but exclude noise



Compression
For data compression:

Compression rate: \(\frac{K}{D} \times 100\%\)
Distortion: Measured by \(\frac{\sum_{d=K+1}^D \lambda_d}{\sum_{d=1}^D \lambda_d} \times 100\%\)
Trade-off: Compression rate vs reconstruction quality

title: Exam questions
text:
Advanced Approaches and Considerations

Cross-Validation

Validation Method
To avoid overfitting, cross-validation can be used:

Divide data into training and test sets
Calculate PCA on training set
Evaluate reconstruction error on test set
Choose \(K\) minimizing test error

Advantage: More robust, especially for small samples



Information Criteria

Akaike (AIC) and BIC Criteria
For normally distributed data, information criteria can be used:

AIC: Balances fit quality and complexity
BIC: More strongly penalizes complexity

These criteria formulate the choice of \(K\) as a model selection problem.



Domain Considerations

Domain Knowledge
Sometimes external considerations guide the choice of \(K\):

Interpretability: Limit to number of components easy to interpret
Technical constraints: Storage or processing limitations
Application requirements: Some applications require specific number of dimensions
